content:
COLLEGE  OF ENGINEERING AND 
TECHNOLOGY 
     DEPARTMENT OF HORTICALTURE 
            EMERGING TECHNOLGY  ASSIGNMENT 
 
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) IN CROP MONITORING 
                       Table of Contents 
1, Introduction 
2, Concept and Meaning of Artificial Intelligence 
3, Overview of Crop Monitoring 
 4, Need for AI in Modern Agriculture 
 5, Components of AI-Based Crop Monitoring Systems 
6 , Applications of AI in Crop Monitoring  
6.1 AI in Soil Monitoring 

6.2 AI in Crop Growth and Health Monitoring 
6.3 AI in Pest, Disease, and Weed Detection 
6.4 AI in Irrigation and Water Management 
6.5 AI in Nutrient and Fertilizer Management 
6.6 AI in Yield Prediction and Forecasting 
Role of Remote Sensing and GIS in AI-Based Crop Monitoring 
Benefits of AI in Crop Monitoring 
Challenges and Limitations of AI in Crop Monitoring 
Future Prospects of AI in Crop Monitoring 
Conclusion 
1. Introduction 
Agriculture is the backbone of many developing economies and 
plays a vital role in ensuring food security, employment, and 
sustainable livelihoods. However, traditional farming practices 
face numerous challenges such as climate change, soil 
degradation, pest outbreaks, water scarcity, and low productivity. 
To overcome these challenges, modern agriculture increasingly 
relies on advanced technologies. Among these technologies, 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in 
crop monitoring. 
Crop monitoring refers to the continuous observation and 
assessment of crop conditions throughout the growing season. It 
involves tracking crop growth, health, soil conditions, weather 
patterns, pest infestations, and yield potential. Artificial 
Intelligence enhances crop monitoring by enabling accurate, real-

time, and data-driven decision-making. AI systems can analyze 
large volumes of agricultural data, identify patterns, and provide 
actionable insights to farmers and agricultural experts. 
The integration of AI into crop monitoring has the potential to 
revolutionize agriculture by improving productivity, reducing costs, 
minimizing environmental impact, and supporting sustainable 
farming practices. This document provides a detailed and 
comprehensive explanation of the role of Artificial Intelligence in 
crop monitoring. 
2. Concept and Meaning of Artificial Intelligence 
Artificial Intelligence refers to the ability of machines and 
computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human 
intelligence. These tasks include learning from experience, 
recognizing patterns, making decisions, solving problems, and 
understanding complex data. AI systems are designed to mimic 
human cognitive functions through algorithms, models, and 
computational techniques. 
Key subfields of Artificial Intelligence include: 
Machine Learning (ML): Enables systems to learn from data and 
improve performance without explicit programming. 
Deep Learning (DL): A subset of machine learning that uses 
artificial neural networks to process complex data such as images 
and satellite imagery. 
Computer Vision: Allows machines to interpret and analyze visual 
information such as crop images. 

Natural Language Processing (NLP): Enables systems to 
understand and process human language, useful for advisory 
services. 
In agriculture, AI combines these techniques to analyze data 
collected from farms, satellites, sensors, and drones. This 
analysis supports accurate crop monitoring and informed 
decision-making. 
3. Overview of Crop Monitoring 
Crop monitoring is the systematic observation of crop conditions 
from planting to harvesting. It aims to ensure optimal crop growth 
and early detection of problems that may affect yield and quality. 
Traditional crop monitoring relies on manual field inspections, 
which are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and often inaccurate. 
Modern crop monitoring involves the use of digital tools such as 
sensors, satellite images, drones, and mobile applications. These 
tools generate large volumes of data related to crop health, soil 
moisture, nutrient status, weather conditions, and pest activity. 
Artificial Intelligence plays a crucial role in analyzing this data and 
converting it into meaningful insights. 
 
Effective crop monitoring helps farmers: 
Detect stress in crops at an early stage 
Optimize irrigation and fertilization 
Control pests and diseases 
Improve yield and crop quality 
Reduce production risks 

4. Need for AI in Modern Agriculture 
The growing global population and changing climate conditions 
have increased pressure on agricultural systems. Farmers must 
produce more food using limited land, water, and resources. 
Traditional farming methods are insufficient to meet these 
demands. 
Artificial Intelligence is needed in modern agriculture because: 
Agricultural data is complex and large in volume 
Weather patterns are unpredictable 
Crop diseases and pests evolve rapidly 
Resources such as water and fertilizers must be used efficiently 
AI enables precision agriculture, where farming practices are 
tailored to specific crop and field conditions. This approach 
improves productivity while minimizing environmental impact. 
5. Components of AI-Based Crop Monitoring Systems 
AI-based crop monitoring systems consist of several 
interconnected components: 
5.1 Data Collection 
Data is collected from various sources including: 
Soil sensors 
Weather stations 
Satellites 
Drones 
Farm machinery 

5.2 Data Processing 
AI algorithms process raw data to remove errors, normalize 
values, and prepare it for analysis. 
5.3 Data Analysis and Modeling 
Machine learning and deep learning models analyze processed 
data to detect patterns, predict outcomes, and identify anomalies. 
5.4 Decision Support Systems 
AI provides recommendations to farmers regarding irrigation, 
fertilization, pest control, and harvesting. 
6. Applications of AI in Crop Monitoring 
6.1 AI in Soil Monitoring 
AI systems analyze soil data such as moisture content, 
temperature, pH, and nutrient levels. This helps in understanding 
soil health and variability within fields. AI-based soil monitoring 
supports site-specific management practices, ensuring optimal 
conditions for crop growth. 
6.2 AI in Crop Growth and Health Monitoring 
Computer vision and deep learning models analyze images from 
drones and satellites to assess crop growth stages and detect 
stress. AI can identify nutrient deficiencies, water stress, and 
growth abnormalities long before they are visible to the human 
eye. 
 

6.3 AI in Pest, Disease, and Weed Detection 
AI-powered image recognition systems can identify pests, 
diseases, and weeds accurately. Early detection allows timely 
intervention, reducing crop losses and minimizing pesticide use. 
6.4 AI in Irrigation and Water Management 
AI analyzes weather forecasts, soil moisture data, and crop water 
requirements to optimize irrigation schedules. This ensures 
efficient water use and prevents over-irrigation or water stress. 
6.5 AI in Nutrient and Fertilizer Management 
AI models recommend the right type and amount of fertilizers 
based on soil and crop data. This improves nutrient use efficiency 
and reduces environmental pollution. 
6.6 AI in Yield Prediction and Forecasting 
AI uses historical and real-time data to predict crop yield 
accurately. Yield forecasting helps farmers plan harvesting, 
storage, and marketing activities. 
7. Role of Remote Sensing and GIS in AI-Based Crop 
Monitoring 
Remote sensing technologies such as satellites and drones 
provide large-scale and high-resolution data on crop conditions. 
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) integrate spatial data with 
AI models to analyze variability across fields and regions. 
AI-enhanced remote sensing enables: 
Monitoring of crop health over large areas 
Detection of stress patterns 
Mapping of yield variability 

8. Benefits of AI in Crop Monitoring 
The use of AI in crop monitoring offers several benefits: 
Increased crop productivity 
Reduced input costs 
Improved resource efficiency 
Early detection of crop problems 
Enhanced sustainability 
Better decision-making 
 
9. Challenges and Limitations of AI in Crop Monitoring 
Despite its benefits, AI in crop monitoring faces challenges such 
as: 
High initial investment costs 
Limited access to technology in developing regions 
Data quality and availability issues 
Need for technical skills and training 
Privacy and data security concerns 
10. Future Prospects of AI in Crop Monitoring 
The future of AI in crop monitoring is promising. Advances in 
sensor technology, cloud computing, and data analytics will 
further enhance AI capabilities. AI is expected to support climate-
smart agriculture, autonomous farming systems, and real-time 
advisory services for farmers. 

11. Conclusion 
Artificial Intelligence has become a powerful tool in crop 
monitoring, transforming traditional agriculture into a data-driven 
and precision-based system. By integrating AI with modern 
technologies such as remote sensing, IoT, and GIS, farmers can 
monitor crops more accurately and efficiently. AI-based crop 
monitoring improves productivity, sustainability, and resilience of 
agricultural systems. Although challenges remain, continued 
innovation and investment will ensure that AI plays a central role 
in the future of agriculture.

Countries. FAO, Rome.

title: Hotel Booking Documentation
author: Amare Agerneh
content:
Hotel Booking System Database 
Documentation 
Overview 
This system is designed to manage hotels, rooms, users, bookings, and 
payments with a focus on data integrity, concurrency control, and 
auditing. It leverages InnoDB features in MySQL such as foreign keys, 
transactions, row-level locking, and JSON columns for flexible data 
storage. 
 
Tables and Relationships 
1. Users 
 Stores system users including customers and administrators. 
 Fields: 
o id: Primary key. 
o name, email, phone: Personal information. 
o password_hash: Secure password storage. 
o role: User type (USER or ADMIN). 
o created_at, updated_at: Timestamps. 
 Constraints: 
o Unique email. 
 Usage: 
o Linked to bookings and transaction logs. 
2. Hotels 
 Stores hotel information. 
 Fields: 
o id, name, address, city, state, country, 
zip_code. 

o rating: Average hotel rating. 
o amenities: JSON array to store dynamic features. 
o description: Optional description of the hotel. 
 Usage: 
o One-to-many relationship with rooms. 
3. Room Types 
 Defines room characteristics for multiple hotels. 
 Fields: 
o id, name, description, capacity, base_price, 
amenities, size_sqft, bed_type. 
 Usage: 
o Linked to rooms table to define the type of each room. 
4. Rooms 
 Represents individual rooms in a hotel. 
 Fields: 
o id, hotel_id, room_type_id, room_number, 
floor, status. 
 Constraints: 
o Unique room number per hotel. 
o Foreign key to hotels (CASCADE on delete). 
o Foreign key to room_types (RESTRICT on delete). 
 Indices: 
o Room status for fast availability searches. 
 Usage: 
o Linked to bookings. 
5. Bookings 
 Records customer reservations. 
 Fields: 

o id, user_id, room_id, checkin_date, 
checkout_date, total_price, status, 
guest_count, special_requests. 
 Constraints: 
o Check constraint ensures checkout_date > 
checkin_date. 
o Foreign keys to users (CASCADE) and rooms 
(RESTRICT). 
 Indices: 
o Optimized for room availability and user booking history. 
 Usage: 
o Central table for booking management. 
 Advanced Techniques: 
o Row-level locks (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) during 
booking creation to prevent double-booking. 
6. Payments 
 Handles payment transactions for bookings. 
 Fields: 
o id, booking_id, amount, currency, method, 
status, transaction_ref, payment_details. 
 Constraints: 
o Foreign key to bookings (CASCADE). 
o Unique transaction reference. 
 Indices: 
o Optimized for booking-based queries. 
 Usage: 
o Integrates financial transactions with bookings. 
 Advanced Techniques: 
o Supports multiple payment methods with JSON storage for 
dynamic details. 
7. Transaction Log 

 Auditing table for all critical actions. 
 Fields: 
o id, booking_id, user_id, action, table_name, 
record_id, old_values, new_values, details, 
ip_address, user_agent. 
 Usage: 
o Tracks changes for compliance and debugging. 
 Advanced Techniques: 
o Stores before/after values in JSON. 
o Foreign keys to bookings and users. 
 
Table Relationships 
 Users → Bookings: One-to-many (users.id → 
bookings.user_id) 
 Hotels → Rooms: One-to-many (hotels.id → 
rooms.hotel_id) 
 Room Types → Rooms: One-to-many (room_types.id → 
rooms.room_type_id) 
 Rooms → Bookings: One-to-many (rooms.id → 
bookings.room_id) 
 Bookings → Payments: One-to-one (bookings.id → 
payments.booking_id) 
 Bookings / Users → Transaction Log: One-to-many 
(bookings.id → transaction_log.booking_id, 
users.id → transaction_log.user_id) 
This structure ensures referential integrity while enabling cascading 
deletions and updates where appropriate. 
 
Advanced Database Techniques 

1. Transactional Integrity 
 Bookings are created inside transactions to ensure atomicity. 
 If any step fails, the transaction rolls back. 
 Guarantees that room availability, payment, and transaction logs 
are synchronized. 
2. Row-Level Locking 
 SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks specific room rows during 
booking. 
 Prevents race conditions where two users book the same room 
simultaneously. 
3. Overlapping Booking Checks 
 SQL checks overlapping dates to prevent double-booking. 
 Uses a condition: 
 NOT (checkout_date <= checkin_date OR 
checkin_date >= checkout_date) 
4. Auditing and Logging 
 Every booking action is logged with old/new values and metadata 
(IP, user agent). 
 Supports tracing, rollback, and compliance reporting. 
5. JSON Columns 
 Flexible storage for amenities and payment_details. 
 Supports dynamic attributes without altering schema. 
 Indexing possible for efficient querying using generated columns 
if needed. 
6. Data Consistency with Foreign Keys 

 Cascading deletes for dependent data (users → bookings → 
payments). 
 Restriction prevents deletion of critical reference data (room_types 
→ rooms). 
 
Stored Procedure: Atomic Booking 
 sp_create_booking handles booking creation atomically: 
1. Locks the room row to prevent concurrent bookings. 
2. Checks for overlapping bookings. 
3. Inserts booking and payment records. 
4. Updates room status to OCCUPIED. 
5. Logs the transaction. 
 Returns success status and descriptive message. 
 Uses exception handling and ROLLBACK to maintain integrity 
on errors. 
 
Summary 
This database is designed for robust hotel booking operations. By 
combining: 
 Foreign key constraints for integrity 
 Transactions for atomic operations 
 Row-level locking to prevent conflicts 
 JSON fields for flexible data 
 Audit logs for traceability 
...it ensures high reliability, concurrency safety, and maintainability 
in a hotel booking system. 
 
 

Table Related To Relationship 
users bookings 1 → ∞ 
users transaction_log 1 → ∞ (nullable FK) 
hotels rooms 1 → ∞ 
room_types rooms 1 → ∞ 
rooms bookings 1 → ∞ 
bookings payments 1 → 1 
bookings transaction_log 1 → ∞ (nullable FK)

title: System Admin Reasearch
author: Amare
content:
Chapter One: Overview of Network And System Administrator 
This chapter defines the roles, responsibilities, and philosophy 
behind system and network administration. 
 Introduction to Key Concepts: 
o The "system" in this context refers to both the operating system 
of a computer and the collective set of all computers in a network, 
forming a "human–computer system"—an organized 
collaboration to solve problems or provide services. 
o System and network administration is an engineering branch 
focused on the operational management of these human-
computer systems. It involves setting up networks and ensuring 
they remain operational despite user activities. 
 Defining the Role: 
o A System Administrator (Sys Admin) is responsible for 
maintaining and operating computer systems or networks for an 
organization. The role requires knowledge of operating systems, 
applications, hardware, software troubleshooting, and technical, 
administrative, and socio-psychological skills. 
o System administration is a demanding engineering job, not just an 
administrative one, encompassing hardware, software, user 
support, diagnosis, repair, and prevention. 
o Traditionally, system administration referred to managing 
computers regardless of network coupling, while network 
administration now specifically refers to managing network 
infrastructure like routers and switches. 
 Responsibilities and Goals: 

o Key Responsibilities: Adding/removing users and hardware, 
performing backups, installing new software, troubleshooting, 
system monitoring, auditing security, and helping users. 
o Main Goals: Ensuring computing systems run correctly and 
efficiently, and enabling users to perform their work easily and 
efficiently. 
 The System Administrator Account: 
o This account has unrestricted access to all system resources, 
allowing the administrator to perform any task, including creating 
users, resetting passwords, monitoring security, and even 
removing critical system files. 
 Types of Administrators: 
o In large companies, roles are often specialized: Database 
Administrator (data integrity), Network Administrator (network 
infrastructure), Security Administrator (security devices), Web 
Administrator (web services), and Computer Operator (routine 
maintenance). In smaller organizations, a few or even one person 
may handle all tasks. 
 Challenges and Job Nature: 
o Challenges: Designing efficient networks, deploying easily 
upgradable machines, deciding necessary services, implementing 
adequate security, and developing error-fixing methods. 
o Job Characteristics: The job is described as complex, painful, 
annoying, highly interactive, well-paid, employable, and often 
thankless. 
 The Philosophy of System Administration: 
This is a set of underlying themes that guide successful 
administration: 

1. Automate Everything: Tasks done more than once (e.g., 
checking disk space, backups) should be automated to save time 
and prevent human error. 
2. Document Everything: Policies, procedures, and changes must 
be documented to avoid confusion in the future. 
3. Communicate as Much as Possible: Inform users about planned, 
current, and completed actions using effective methods like email 
or internal websites. 
4. Know Your Resources: Understand and balance system resources 
(processing power, memory, disk space), network bandwidth, and 
the IT budget. 
5. Know Your Users: Understand the people who use the systems, 
identifying power users and learning about their needs. 
6. Know Your Business: Understand the purpose of the systems 
you manage and the nature of the organization you work for. 
7. Make the Systems Secure: Consider potential threats, the value 
of data, and authorized access to implement appropriate security. 
8. Plan Ahead: Anticipate future developments and changes when 
installing networks and resources. 
9. Expect the Unexpected: Anticipate potential problems (e.g., 
hardware failure) to respond quickly and effectively. 
 
Chapter Two: Windows Server Network Concepts 
This chapter explains fundamental Windows networking concepts, 
focusing on workgroups, domains, and Active Directory. 
 Workgroup: 

o A workgroup is a peer-to-peer (P2P) grouping of computers on a 
LAN that share resources like files and printers. 
o It is designed for small networks (best with 15 or fewer 
computers) and functions without a dedicated server. 
o All computers in a workgroup must have a unique computer 
name but share the same workgroup name. 
o As the network grows, workgroups become difficult to administer 
and should be replaced with a domain model. 
 Server Domain: 
o A domain is a logical group of network objects (computers, users, 
devices) that share a common Active Directory database. It acts as 
a management boundary. 
o In a domain, one or more servers act as domain controllers, 
allowing administrators to centrally manage security and 
permissions for all computers. Users can log on to any computer 
in the domain with a single domain user account. 
o A key disadvantage is that if the domain controller fails, the entire 
network can go down (a single point of failure). 
 Active Directory (AD): 
o AD is a directory structure used in Windows to store information 
about networks and domains. It organizes objects for easy 
retrieval, provides access for users and administrators, and allows 
for security settings. 
o The AD structure is hierarchical, consisting of Forests (the top 
level), Trees (collections of domains), and Domains (logical 
groups). 
o Objects: AD stores different types of objects, 
including Computers (domain controllers, servers, 

workstations), Groups (security groups for permissions, 
distribution groups for email), and Users. 
o Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS): When installed on a 
Windows Server, it turns the server into a Domain Controller 
(DC) , enabling it to centrally manage, authenticate, and provide 
services to all member computers. 
 Structure of Active Directory: 
o Logical Structure: Defines how objects are organized. 
 Domain: A logical group of objects sharing the same AD 
database. 
 Tree: A collection of one or more domains. 
 Forest: A collection of trees that share a common schema and 
global catalog, representing a security boundary. 
 Organizational Units (OUs): Subdivisions within a domain used 
to create hierarchy and delegate administrative powers. 
o Physical Structure: Defines the network topology. 
 Site: A set of well-connected subnets representing the physical 
network structure. 
 Domain Controller (DC): A server that stores a replica of the 
domain directory and handles security requests. Multiple DCs 
provide fault tolerance. 
 Trust Relationships: 
o A trust is a relationship between domains or forests that allows 
resource sharing. 
o Direction: 
 One-way Trust: Domain A trusts Domain B, allowing B to access 
A's resources. 
 Two-way Trust: Both domains trust each other, allowing mutual 
access. 

o Transitivity: 
 Transitive Trust: Can be extended beyond the initial two domains 
to other domains in the forest. 
 Non-transitive Trust: Exists only between the two domains that 
created it. 
o Types of Trusts: 
 Shortcut Trust: Manually created to improve logon times 
between distant domains (transitive). 
 External Trust: Manually created between domains in separate 
forests or with older Windows NT domains (non-transitive). 
 Realm Trust: Manually created between a Windows domain and 
a non-Microsoft domain (e.g., UNIX). 
 Forest Trust: Manually created between two Windows forests to 
allow all domains in one forest to trust all in another. 
 Tree-root Trust: Automatically created between a new tree and 
its root domain (transitive, two-way). 
 Parent-child Trust: Automatically created between a child 
domain and its parent domain (transitive, two-way). 
 
Short Summary 
This document provides a foundational overview of system and 
network administration, divided into two parts. 
Part 1: System Administration Overview 
It defines system administration as the engineering of human-
computer systems, involving the setup and maintenance of 
networks and hardware. A system administrator is responsible for 

tasks like user management, backups, troubleshooting, and 
security, with the core goals of ensuring system efficiency and 
user productivity. The role is complex, often thankless, but highly 
skilled and well-paid. The chapter concludes with a philosophy for 
successful administration, emphasizing the importance 
of automation, documentation, communication, knowledge 
of resources/users/business, security, planning, and expecting 
the unexpected. 
Part 2: Windows Network Concepts 
This section contrasts two main ways of organizing Windows 
networks. A workgroup is a small, simple peer-to-peer setup 
suitable for fewer than 15 computers, where each device is 
managed individually. A domain is a larger, centralized model 
where a domain controller manages security and resources for 
all computers through a Active Directory (AD) database. AD has 
a logical structure (forests, trees, domains, and organizational 
units) and a physical structure (sites and domain controllers). To 
allow sharing between different domains or forests, trust 
relationships (e.g., one-way, two-way, transitive, non-transitive) 
are established.

payments). 
 Restriction prevents deletion of critical reference data (room_types 
→ rooms). 
 
Stored Procedure: Atomic Booking 
 sp_create_booking handles booking creation atomically: 
1. Locks the room row to prevent concurrent bookings. 
2. Checks for overlapping bookings. 
3. Inserts booking and payment records. 
4. Updates room status to OCCUPIED. 
5. Logs the transaction. 
 Returns success status and descriptive message. 
 Uses exception handling and ROLLBACK to maintain integrity 
on errors. 
 
Summary 
This database is designed for robust hotel booking operations. By 
combining: 
 Foreign key constraints for integrity 
 Transactions for atomic operations 
 Row-level locking to prevent conflicts 
 JSON fields for flexible data 
 Audit logs for traceability 
...it ensures high reliability, concurrency safety, and maintainability 
in a hotel booking system.

1 ⃣ First: Understand What Your Instructor Really Wants 
Let’s challenge a common mistake first  
Many students jump straight into Packet Tracer and “make it 
work”. That’s not enough. 
Your grading is based on three things: 
1. Correct network design 
2. Correct configuration (OSPF + ACL) 
3. Your understanding and documentation 
So your project has two parallel tracks: 
 A. Packet Tracer Implementation 
 B. Written Documentation (steps + screenshots + 
explanation) 
You must build both together, not separately. 
 
  ⃣ Network Design (VERY IMPORTANT) 
Recommended Simple but Strong Topology 
Do NOT overcomplicate. One router is enough. 
PC1 ---- Switch1 ----| 
                      |---- Router ---- 
Switch2 ---- PC2 
PC3 ---- Switch1 ----| 
Devices to Use 

 1 Router (e.g. Router 2911) 
 2 Switches (2960) 
 3–4 PCs 
Why this works: 
 Multiple networks → OSPF is meaningful 
 Router is central → ACL firewall makes sense 
 Easy to explain during demo 
 
  ⃣ IP Addressing Plan (Before Configuration) 
Never configure without planning IPs first. 
Device Interface IP Address Subnet 
Router G0/0 192.168.1.1 /24 
Router G0/1 192.168.2.1 /24 
PC1 NIC 192.168.1.10 /24 
PC3 NIC 192.168.1.11 /24 
PC2 NIC 192.168.2.10 /24 
Gateway for PCs: 
 Network 1 → 192.168.1.1 
 Network 2 → 192.168.2.1 
 Screenshot this table for your documentation. 
 
  ⃣ Step-by-Step Packet Tracer Implementation 

  Step 1: Physical Setup 
1. Place router, switches, PCs 
2. Use Copper Straight-Through cables 
3. Connect: 
o PCs → Switches 
o Switches → Router 
 Screenshot: Physical topology 
 
  Step 2: Configure IP Addresses on PCs 
For each PC: 
 Desktop → IP Configuration 
 Enter IP, subnet, gateway 
 Screenshot: PC IP configuration 
 
  Step 3: Configure Router Interfaces 
On the router (CLI): 
enable 
configure terminal 
 
interface g0/0 
ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0 
no shutdown 
exit 

 
interface g0/1 
ip address 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0 
no shutdown 
exit 
 Screenshot: Router interface configuration 
 
  ⃣ Objective 1: OSPF Routing Configuration 
Why OSPF? 
You must be able to answer this: 
“OSPF is a dynamic link-state routing protocol that 
automatically updates routing tables, making the network 
scalable and fault tolerant.” 
Configure OSPF on Router 
router ospf 1 
network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 
network 192.168.2.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 
exit 
Verify: 
show ip route 
You should see routes marked with O. 
 Screenshot: 

 OSPF configuration 
 Routing table output 
 Devil’s advocate: 
If you only have one router, why OSPF? 
Answer during demo: 
“This simulates a scalable network. OSPF is implemented to 
demonstrate dynamic routing principles, even though the 
topology is small.” 
That answer saves you marks. 
 
  ⃣ Objective 2: Firewall Security Using ACL 
Scenario (Keep It Simple) 
 Allow PC1 to access PC2 
 Deny PC3 from accessing PC2 
Standard ACL Example 
access-list 10 deny host 192.168.1.11 
access-list 10 permit any 
Apply ACL to router interface towards destination network: 
interface g0/1 
ip access-group 10 out 
exit 
Testing 

 PC1 → ping PC2  
 PC3 → ping PC2  
 Screenshot: 
 ACL configuration 
 Successful and failed ping tests 
 
  ⃣ Documentation Structure (VERY IMPORTANT) 
Your report should follow this structure: 
1. Introduction 
 Brief overview of the project 
 Objectives (OSPF + ACL) 
2. Network Topology 
 Diagram (Packet Tracer screenshot) 
 Devices used 
3. IP Addressing Scheme 
 Table (like above) 
4. OSPF Configuration 
 Commands used 
 Explanation 
 Screenshot 
5. Firewall (ACL) Configuration 

 Security goal 
 ACL commands 
 Test results 
6. Conclusion 
 What you learned 
 Importance of OSPF and firewall security 
 
  ⃣ How to Prepare for Evaluation  
Each group member must answer: 
 What is OSPF? 
 Why area 0? 
 Difference between static routing and OSPF 
 Why ACL applied on outbound, not inbound 
 What happens if ACL order is changed?

What is a network topology? 
 In communication networks, a topology is a usually schematic

below:

In a bus topology, all devices attach to the same

All buses are implemented using electrical cable, 
usually coax, and the ends of the cable must be 
terminated with a terminating resistor that matches 
the impedance of the cable.  
The terminating resistor prevents data reflections from 
coming across as data corruption. 
 The bus is considered a multipoint system because all 
devices tap into the same backbone cable. 

11/10/2025 
27 
An important characteristic to remember in bus 
topologies is that all data signals are broadcast 
throughout the bus structure. 
 In the following diagram, if node B sends a signal to 
node C, the signal propagates for the length of the 
cable and is seen by nodes A and D as well.  
It is necessary to have an addressing mechanism so that 
each node understands which messages it is to receive 
and which to ignore.

In a star topology all stations are wired to a

4. Mesh topology  
How it works 
•Each device, or node, is connected to multiple other 
nodes.  
•There is no single central point of connection.  
•Data is sent between nodes, with each node capable 
of relaying the message to its destination.  
•Routing algorithms determine the most efficient path, 
and if a link is down, the data can automatically take an 
alternative route.  
•This creates a "self-healing" network that is resilient to 
single points of failure.

Advantages 
•High reliability and fault tolerance: 
If one connection fails, alternative paths exist for data to reach its 
destination.  
•Resilience:

complete network breakdown.  
•Multiple paths: 
Data can travel through several routes, which can help prevent 
network congestion.  
•Security: 
Data can be routed through secure paths, making the network 
more secure.  

 
Disadvantages 
•High cost:

hardware.  
•Complex setup:

difficult, especially as the number of nodes grows.  
•Requires more space:

physical space.  
•High power consumption:

as a router, receiving and sending message

1.5: Host Connectivity 

11/10/2025 
51 
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 
This section covers peer-to-peer networks.  
When LAN and WAN technologies are used, many 
computers are interconnected to provide services to 
their users.  
To accomplish this, networked computers take on 
different roles or functions in relation to each other. 
Some types of applications require computers to 
function as equal partners. 
 Other types of applications distribute their work so 
that one computer functions to serve a number of 
others in an unequal relationship.  

11/10/2025 
52 
Two computers generally use request and response 
protocols to communicate with each other.  
 
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 

11/10/2025 
53 
One computer issues a request for a service, and a second 
computer receives and responds to that request.  
The requestor acts like a client and the responder acts like 
a server. 
 In a peer-to-peer network, networked computers act as 
equal partners, or peers.  
As peers, each computer can take on the client function or 
the server function. Computer A may request for a file 
from Computer B, which then sends the file to Computer 
A. Computer A acts like the client and Computer B acts 
like the server. At a later time, Computers A and B can 
reverse roles.  
 
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 

11/10/2025 
54 
In a peer-to-peer network: 
 individual users control their own resources.  
The users may decide to share certain files with other users. 
 The users may also require passwords before they allow 
others to access their resources. Since individual users make 
these decisions, there is no central point of control or 
administration in the network. 
 In addition, individual users must back up their own systems 
to be able to recover from data loss in case of failures. When a 
computer acts as a server, the user of that machine may 
experience reduced performance as the machine serves the 
requests made by other systems.  
 
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 

11/10/2025 
55 
Peer-to-peer networks are relatively easy to install and 
operate.  
No additional equipment is necessary beyond a suitable 
operating system installed on each computer.  
Since users control their own resources, no dedicated 
administrators are needed.  
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 

11/10/2025 
56 
As networks grow, peer-to-peer relationships become 
increasingly difficult to coordinate.  
A peer-to-peer network works well with ten or fewer 
computers. Since peer-to-peer networks do not scale well, 
their efficiency decreases rapidly as the number of 
computers on the network increases.  
Also, individual users control access to the resources on 
their computers, which means security may be difficult to 
maintain.  
The client/server model of networking can be used to 
overcome the limitations of the peer-to-peer network  
A.  Peer-to-Peer Networks 

11/10/2025 
57 
B. Client/Server Networks 
In a client/server arrangement, network services are 
located on a dedicated computer called a server.  
The server responds to the requests of clients.  
The server is a central computer that is continuously 
available to respond to requests from clients for file, 
print, application, and other services.  
Most network operating systems adopt the form of a 
client/server relationship. 
 Typically, desktop computers function as clients and one 
or more computers with additional processing power, 
memory, and specialized software function as servers.  

11/10/2025 
58 
Client/Server Networks 

Client/Server Networks 
 
11/10/2025 
59 

Client/Server Networks 
 
11/10/2025 
60 

11/10/2025 
61 
Client/Server Networks 
Servers are designed to handle requests from many 
clients simultaneously. 
 Before a client can access the server resources, the 
client must be identified and be authorized to use the 
resource.  
Each client is assigned an account name and password 
that is verified by an authentication service. 
 The authentication service guards access to the 
network. With the centralization of user accounts, 
security, and access control, server-based networks 
simplify the administration of large networks.  

11/10/2025 
62 
Client/Server Networks 
The concentration of network resources such as files, printers, and 
applications on servers also makes it easier to back-up and maintain 
the data. 
 Resources can be located on specialized, dedicated servers for easier 
access.  
Most client/server systems also include ways to enhance the network 
with new services that extend the usefulness of the network.  
The centralized functions in a client/server network has substantial 
advantages and some disadvantages.  
Although a centralized server enhances security, ease of access, and 
control, it introduces a single point of failure into the network. 
Without an operational server, the network cannot function at all. 
 Servers require a trained, expert staff member to administer and 
maintain. Server systems also require additional hardware and 
specialized software that add to the cost  

11/10/2025 
63 
Advantages and Disadvantages of Peer-to-
Peer and Client/Server Networks 

11/10/2025 
64 
Advantage and disadvantage cont... 

 
1.6: Basic Data Communication 
Hardware Devices 
11/10/2025 
65

66 

 
1.6.1. NIC /Network Interface 
Card/Adapter Card: 
 
 
 
11/10/2025 
67 

Devices cont... 
11/10/2025 
68 

NIC cont... 
A NIC, or LAN adapter, provides network 
communication capabilities to and from a PC. 
On desktop computer systems, it is a printed circuit 
board that resides in a slot on the motherboard and 
provides an interface connection to the network media. 
On laptop computer systems, it is commonly integrated 
into the laptop or available on a small, credit card-sized 
PCMCIA card.    
PCMCIA stands for Personal Computer Memory Card 
International Association.  
 
 
11/10/2025 
69 

NIC cont... 
The function of a NIC is to connect a host 
device to the network medium.  
A NIC is a printed circuit board that fits into 
the expansion slot on the motherboard or 
peripheral device of a computer.  
The NIC is also referred to as a network 
adapter. On laptop or notebook computers a 
NIC is the size of a credit card. 
 
11/10/2025

NIC and Modem Installation 
Modem – Modulator/Demodulator 
Used to convert data from digital to analog and vice versa 
Modems could be internal or external 
For dialup networking we use modems 
NICs must be installed before a PC can communicate with other PCs 
on a network 
Situations that require NIC installation include the following: 
Installation of a NIC on a PC that does not already have one  
Replacement of a malfunctioning or damaged NIC

Bridges and switches operate at the Data Link layer. 
When a bridge receives a frame on the network, the destination 
MAC address is looked up in the bridge table to determine whether 
to filter, flood, or copy the frame onto another segment.  
This decision process occurs as follows:   
If the destination device is on the same segment as the frame, the bridge 
will not send the frame onto other segments. This process is known as 
filtering.  
If the destination device is on a different segment, the bridge forwards 
the frame to the appropriate segment.  
If the destination address is unknown to the bridge, the bridge forwards 
the frame to all segments except the one on which it was received. This 
process is known as flooding.
